title: Frege and Russell: The Logic Revolution
subtitle: How a quiet German mathematician and a famous English aristocrat rebuilt logic and taught philosophy to analyze
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain why Frege's new logic was the biggest advance in the subject since Aristotle
Use Frege's distinction between sense and reference to explain why 'the morning star is the evening star' is informative
Explain Russell's theory of descriptions and how it handles 'The present King of France is bald'
State Russell's paradox and explain why it devastated Frege's project
Describe 'analysis' as a philosophical method and the beginnings of the analytic tradition
hook:
June 1902. In the small university town of Jena, a fifty-three-year-old mathematics professor named Gottlob Frege is putting the finishing touches to the second volume of his life's work, *Basic Laws of Arithmetic*. For more than two decades he has been trying to prove that all of arithmetic can be built from pure logic. Few people have read his books; even fewer have understood them. Then a letter arrives from a young Englishman named Bertrand Russell. It is polite, admiring, and lethal. Russell writes that he agrees with Frege on almost everything, but he has found a contradiction at the heart of the system.

Frege wrote back within days. He admitted that the discovery had left him thunderstruck, because it shook the very foundation on which he had meant to build arithmetic. He added an appendix to his book acknowledging the problem. Russell later wrote that he knew of nothing to equal Frege's dedication to truth: his life's work was on the verge of completion, and his response to learning it was flawed was intellectual pleasure at the new problem rather than despair. Today we meet these two men, the logic they created, and the paradox that linked them forever. Their work opens our new unit on the **analytic tradition**, the style of philosophy that dominates most English-speaking universities today.

sections.heading: Why Logic Needed a Revolution
sections.body:
Remember Aristotle's syllogism from Day 17? All humans are mortal; Socrates is a human; therefore Socrates is mortal. For over two thousand years, Aristotle's logic was treated as essentially complete. Kant (Day 55) even said that logic had not been able to take a single step forward since Aristotle.

But syllogistic logic had serious limits. It handled sentences of the form "All A are B" and "Some A are B" well, but struggled with relations and with sentences that mix "all" and "some." Consider: "Everyone loves someone." That could mean each person loves at least one person (perhaps different people), or that there is one lucky person whom everyone loves. These are very different claims, and Aristotle's system had no clean way to tell them apart. Mathematics is full of such sentences: "For every number, there is a larger number." A logic that could not handle them could not capture mathematical reasoning.

The nineteenth century saw several attempts at improvement. The English mathematician George Boole, in *The Laws of Thought* (1854), treated logic as a kind of algebra. But the decisive breakthrough came from Frege.

sections.heading: Frege: The Concept-Script and the Birth of Modern Logic
sections.body:
Gottlob Frege (1848–1925) spent nearly his whole career teaching mathematics at the University of Jena. He was shy, conservative and largely ignored in his lifetime. Yet in a slim book of 1879 called *Begriffsschrift* ("Concept-Script") he invented what we now call **predicate logic**, the foundation of all modern logic.

Frege's key innovation was the **quantifier**: precise symbols for "for all" and "there exists," which can be stacked and combined. With them, the two meanings of "Everyone loves someone" become:

1. For every person x, there exists a person y such that x loves y.
2. There exists a person y such that, for every person x, x loves y.

The order of the quantifiers makes the difference visible. Frege also analyzed sentences not as subject and predicate, in the grammatical way, but as **functions** and **arguments**, borrowing an idea from mathematics. "Socrates is wise" applies the function "x is wise" to the argument Socrates.

Why did Frege want this? His goal was **logicism**: the thesis that arithmetic is really just logic in disguise, that numbers and their laws can be defined and proved using purely logical concepts. If he succeeded, arithmetic would be certain, and Kant would be wrong that arithmetic truths are synthetic a priori (Day 55). They would be analytic, true by logic alone. In *The Foundations of Arithmetic* (1884), a brilliant and witty book, he demolished earlier theories of number, mocking the idea that numbers are piles of pebbles or mental images, and sketched his own definition: roughly, the number of a concept is the class of all concepts that can be put into one-to-one correspondence with it.

In the same book he stated a principle that would echo through the century: never ask for the meaning of a word in isolation, but only in the context of a sentence. Wittgenstein (Days 70 and 73) would take that thought in directions Frege never imagined.

sections.heading: Sense and Reference: The Morning Star and the Evening Star
sections.body:
Frege's most famous essay, "On Sense and Reference" (1892), begins with a puzzle that sounds trivial but is not.

The ancients saw a bright star in the east before dawn and called it the Morning Star (Phosphorus). They saw a bright star in the west after sunset and called it the Evening Star (Hesperus). Eventually astronomers discovered that both were the same object: the planet Venus.

Now compare two sentences:

- "The Morning Star is the Morning Star."
- "The Morning Star is the Evening Star."

If the meaning of a name were simply the object it names, these sentences would mean exactly the same thing, since both say Venus is Venus. Yet the first is trivial, knowable without looking at the sky, while the second was a real astronomical discovery. How can that be?

Frege's answer was to distinguish two aspects of meaning. The **reference** (in German, *Bedeutung*) of an expression is the thing it picks out: here, Venus. The **sense** (*Sinn*) is the *way* it picks out that thing, its "mode of presentation": the bright body seen at dawn versus the bright body seen at dusk. The two names share a reference but differ in sense. That is why learning that they co-refer is real knowledge.

An everyday example: "the author of the Harry Potter books" and "the richest writer in Britain" may refer to the same person, but someone could know one description without knowing the other. Sense is what you grasp when you understand an expression; reference is what in the world it hooks onto.

Frege extended the idea to whole sentences, more controversially: a sentence's sense is the thought it expresses, and its reference, he argued, is its truth value, the True or the False. And he insisted that senses and thoughts are not private mental images. Two people can grasp the very same thought, which is what makes communication and science possible. This anti-psychologism, the refusal to reduce logic to psychology, became a hallmark of analytic philosophy.

sections.heading: Russell's Paradox: The Crack in the Foundations
sections.body:
Bertrand Russell (1872–1970) was everything Frege was not: an aristocrat (the grandson of a British prime minister), a public celebrity, a lifelong political campaigner and a prolific, witty writer. In 1900 he discovered the new logic, first through the Italian mathematician Giuseppe Peano and soon through Frege, and he set out on the same logicist project.

In 1901 he found a problem. Frege's system, like ordinary thinking, assumed that any well-defined condition determines a **set** (or class): the set of all red things, the set of all even numbers, and so on. Some sets seem to be members of themselves. The set of all things that are not teacups is not a teacup, so it is a member of itself. Most sets, like the set of teacups, are not members of themselves.

Now consider the set of all sets that are *not* members of themselves. Call it R. Is R a member of itself?

- If R is a member of itself, then it fails the condition for membership, so it is *not* a member of itself.
- If R is not a member of itself, then it meets the condition, so it *is* a member of itself.

Either answer implies its opposite. This is **Russell's paradox**. Russell sometimes illustrated it with a village barber who shaves all and only those villagers who do not shave themselves. Who shaves the barber? (Strictly, the barber version just shows such a barber cannot exist; the set version is worse, because Frege's logic seemed to *guarantee* that set R exists.)

A contradiction at the base of a logical system is catastrophic: from a contradiction, anything at all can be proved. Frege's Basic Law V, the axiom that let him form sets from any concept, was the culprit. He never found a satisfying repair, and late in life he abandoned logicism.

Russell's own solution was the **theory of types**: sets are arranged in a hierarchy, and a set can only contain items from the level below it, so the question "Is R a member of itself?" cannot even be properly asked. With Alfred North Whitehead he then spent a decade writing *Principia Mathematica* (three volumes, 1910–1913), an enormous attempt to derive mathematics from logic. Its proof that 1 + 1 = 2 arrives famously late, hundreds of pages into the work. In 1931 the young Austrian logician Kurt Gödel proved his incompleteness theorems, showing that any consistent formal system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. The dream of capturing all mathematical truth in one complete system of logic was over.

sections.heading: The Present King of France Is Bald: Russell's Theory of Descriptions
sections.body:
Russell's most celebrated piece of philosophy appeared in a 1905 article, "On Denoting." It addresses a puzzle that seems almost silly.

Consider: "The present King of France is bald." France has had no king since 1848. So is the sentence true? No: there is no bald King of France. Is it false? Then, by the law of excluded middle (Day 17), "The present King of France is not bald" should be true. But that seems wrong too. We cannot find the king among either the bald or the hairy. Some philosophers, such as the Austrian Alexius Meinong, had concluded that nonexistent objects must have some kind of shadowy being so that we can talk about them. Russell found this an offense against a robust sense of reality.

Russell's solution was to show that the sentence's grammar misleads us about its **logical form**. "The present King of France" looks like a name referring to an object, but it is really a disguised combination of claims. The sentence says:

1. There is at least one present King of France;
2. There is at most one present King of France; and
3. Whoever is present King of France is bald.

Since the first claim is false, the whole sentence is simply false. And "The present King of France is not bald" turns out to be ambiguous: it can mean "There is a unique present King of France who is not bald" (false) or "It is not the case that there is a unique present King of France who is bald" (true). No shadowy kings needed. This is the **theory of descriptions**.

The young Cambridge philosopher Frank Ramsey later called it a paradigm of philosophy. The lesson was general: ordinary grammar can hide the true logical structure of what we say, and many philosophical puzzles arise from being fooled by surface grammar. Not everyone was convinced. In 1950 the Oxford philosopher P.F. Strawson argued that Russell had misdescribed ordinary speech: someone who says the King of France is bald has not said something false but has failed to say anything true or false at all, because the sentence presupposes there is a king. That debate leads straight to the ordinary language philosophy of Day 73.

sections.heading: Analysis as Method and the Birth of a Tradition
sections.body:
Frege and Russell gave philosophy a new method: **analysis**, breaking complex statements and concepts into their simpler logical parts to see what they really say. Russell believed that much of traditional philosophy was confused because it had been led astray by language. Clarify the logical form, and many problems would be solved or dissolved.

This was also a rebellion. Around 1898 Russell and his Cambridge friend G.E. Moore turned against the Hegelian idealism (Day 59) that had dominated British philosophy, represented by F.H. Bradley, who held that reality is a single, unified Absolute and that separate things and relations are ultimately unreal. Moore defended common sense; Russell defended a world of many independent things and facts. He later called his view **logical atomism**: the world consists of simple facts, and a perfect logical language would mirror their structure. Russell said that after the rebellion he felt as if he had escaped from a hothouse onto a windswept headland.

Russell's life outside the study was just as eventful. He was jailed for six months in 1918 for writing against the First World War, and he used the time to write *Introduction to Mathematical Philosophy*. In 1940 a New York court blocked his appointment to teach at the City College of New York because of his views on sex and marriage. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1950, co-wrote the 1955 Russell–Einstein Manifesto against nuclear weapons, and was arrested again at the age of eighty-nine at an anti-nuclear protest. His *History of Western Philosophy* (1945), witty but often unfair, made him rich.

Frege's life ended more darkly. He died in 1925 almost unknown, and diary entries from his last years reveal ugly antisemitic and anti-democratic views, a reminder that brilliance in logic is no guarantee of wisdom in politics. His fame came posthumously, through Russell, Wittgenstein and later scholars.

Between them, they handed the next generation a powerful toolkit and a burning question: if logic reveals the hidden structure of language, what does language reveal about the world? A brilliant, tormented young Austrian who arrived at Russell's door in 1911 would try to answer that question tomorrow.

keyQuote.text: Never ask for the meaning of a word in isolation, but only in the context of a proposition.
keyQuote.source: Gottlob Frege, The Foundations of Arithmetic (1884), Introduction (trans. J.L. Austin; the 'context principle')

modernConnection.title: From Concept-Script to Code: The Logic Inside Your Devices
modernConnection.body:
Frege wrote *Begriffsschrift* to make mathematical reasoning perfectly rigorous. He could not have imagined that his invention would end up running inside nearly every computer on earth.

The road was not direct. It passed through Boole's algebra (the basis of the true/false logic gates in chips), through Gödel, and through Alonzo Church and Alan Turing, who in the 1930s used the precise logical languages descended from Frege and Russell to define exactly what it means to compute. But the family resemblance is everywhere. When you search a database for "all customers who bought something in March," you are using a quantifier: the query language SQL is built on predicate logic. Programming languages such as Haskell and Rust use type systems, distant descendants of Russell's theory of types, to stop programs from doing nonsensical operations, much as Russell's hierarchy stopped sets from containing themselves. Proof assistants such as Lean and Coq now let mathematicians check proofs line by line in a formal language, fulfilling Frege's dream of gap-free reasoning in a way he never could by hand.

Frege's sense and reference shows up too. When a search engine has to work out that "the 44th US president" and "Barack Obama" pick out the same person, it is dealing with two senses that share one reference. Knowledge graphs, which store facts as relations between entities, are built on exactly this distinction.

But the comparison has limits. Gödel showed that no formal system can capture all mathematical truth, and the history of artificial intelligence shows how hard it is to translate the messiness of real human language into tidy logical form. Early AI built on hand-written logical rules struggled; today's large language models learn patterns from text statistically rather than reasoning from explicit axioms. Whether future AI needs more Frege, or less, is one of the live debates in computer science, which we revisit on Days 84 and 89.

vocabulary.definition: The system of formal logic, invented by Frege, that uses quantifiers, predicates and variables to represent the structure of statements, including relations.
vocabulary.example: Predicate logic can distinguish 'everyone loves someone' from 'someone is loved by everyone.'

vocabulary.definition: A logical expression meaning 'for all' (universal) or 'there exists' (existential) that specifies how many things a statement is about.
vocabulary.example: In 'for every number there is a larger number,' the order of the two quantifiers is essential.

vocabulary.definition: The thesis, pursued by Frege and Russell, that mathematics can be derived entirely from logic.
vocabulary.example: Russell's paradox and later Gödel's theorems dealt serious blows to logicism.

vocabulary.definition: Frege's distinction between the object an expression picks out (reference) and the way or mode in which it presents that object (sense).
vocabulary.example: 'The Morning Star' and 'the Evening Star' have the same reference, Venus, but different senses.

vocabulary.definition: The contradiction arising from the set of all sets that are not members of themselves, which is a member of itself if and only if it is not.
vocabulary.example: Russell's paradox showed that not every condition can define a set without leading to contradiction.

vocabulary.definition: Russell's analysis of phrases like 'the so-and-so' as hidden claims that exactly one thing has a certain property, rather than as names.
vocabulary.example: Using the theory of descriptions, 'The present King of France is bald' comes out simply false.

vocabulary.definition: The underlying logical structure of a statement, which may differ from its surface grammatical form.
vocabulary.example: Russell argued that the logical form of 'The present King of France is bald' contains an existence claim.

vocabulary.definition: The philosophical method of breaking down complex statements or concepts into simpler parts to clarify what they really mean.
vocabulary.example: Through analysis, a vague debate about whether 'nothing' exists may turn out to rest on a grammatical confusion.

thinkingExercise.title: Doing Analysis Yourself
thinkingExercise.prompt: Practice the analytic method of Frege and Russell on everyday language. Work through these steps for 10 to 15 minutes, writing your answers.
steps: Write down two different meanings of the sentence 'Every student read a book.' Rewrite each using the phrases 'for every' and 'there exists' to show the difference.

Find a pair of expressions with the same reference but different senses from your own life (for example, 'my mother' and 'the woman who taught my math class'). Write a sentence that would be informative to someone even though it only says that one thing is itself.
Apply Russell's theory of descriptions to 'The tallest person in this room is a doctor.' Break it into its three hidden claims. Under what circumstances would the sentence be false?
Think of a public argument where people seem to be talking past each other because of a hidden ambiguity. Analyze the key phrase into two or more possible logical forms.
Reflect: does analyzing language in this way clear up real problems, or does it risk missing what people actually mean? Write a short paragraph.

summary: Frege's Begriffsschrift (1879) invented predicate logic, with quantifiers that can express relations and multiple generality, the greatest advance in logic since Aristotle.
Frege's distinction between sense and reference explains why identity statements like 'The Morning Star is the Evening Star' can be informative.

Russell's paradox showed a contradiction at the base of Frege's logicist system; Russell responded with the theory of types and Principia Mathematica, but Gödel later showed no formal system can capture all mathematical truth.
Russell's theory of descriptions analyzed 'the so-and-so' as a hidden existence and uniqueness claim, showing how surface grammar can mislead philosophers.
Together, Frege, Russell and Moore launched analytic philosophy, built on logic, clarity and the method of analysis, as a rebellion against Hegelian idealism.

quiz.question: What was Frege's main innovation in the Begriffsschrift (1879)?
options: Quantifiers that let logic handle relations and statements mixing 'all' and 'some'
The idea that logic is a branch of psychology
quiz.explanation: Frege's quantifiers created predicate logic. The syllogism was Aristotle's, dialectic Hegel's, and Frege fiercely opposed psychologism.

quiz.question: Why is 'The Morning Star is the Evening Star' informative while 'The Morning Star is the Morning Star' is trivial, according to Frege?
options: The two names have the same reference but different senses
The two names refer to different objects
Names have no meaning at all outside of sentences
quiz.explanation: Both names refer to Venus, but they present it in different ways, so discovering the identity is real knowledge.

quiz.question: Frege's goal of logicism was to show that arithmetic can be derived from pure logic.
quiz.explanation: Frege aimed to show arithmetic truths are analytic, against Kant's view that they are synthetic a priori.

quiz.question: Which set generates Russell's paradox?
options: The set of all even numbers
The set of all sets that are members of themselves
The set of all sets that are not members of themselves
quiz.explanation: That set is a member of itself if and only if it is not, an outright contradiction.

quiz.question: According to Russell's theory of descriptions, what is the truth value of 'The present King of France is bald'?
options: False, because it implies there is exactly one present King of France
quiz.explanation: Russell analyzed it as including the claim that a unique King of France exists, which is false. Strawson later argued it is neither true nor false.

quiz.question: Russell solved his paradox so thoroughly that Gödel's later work confirmed Principia Mathematica could derive every mathematical truth.
quiz.explanation: Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931) showed that any consistent formal system rich enough for arithmetic has true but unprovable statements.

quiz.question: A website search box treats 'the author of Frankenstein' and 'Mary Shelley' as the same person while storing them as different phrases. Which distinction does this illustrate?
quiz.explanation: The two expressions differ in sense but share a reference, exactly Frege's distinction.

quiz.question: Against which philosophical movement were Russell and Moore rebelling around 1898?
quiz.explanation: They rejected the idealism of F.H. Bradley and others in favor of common sense, many independent things and logical analysis.

quiz.question: What is the core idea of 'analysis' as a philosophical method?
options: Interpreting history as the progress of Spirit
Testing ideas only by their practical consequences
Abandoning reason in favor of faith
Breaking statements and concepts into simpler logical parts to reveal what they really say
quiz.explanation: Frege and Russell believed clarifying logical form could solve or dissolve many philosophical problems.

quiz.question: Frege was a celebrated public figure in his lifetime, widely recognized as the founder of modern logic.
quiz.explanation: Frege was largely ignored during his life; his reputation grew mostly after his death, through Russell, Wittgenstein and later scholars.

goDeeper.body:
The sense/reference distinction launched a century of debate in the philosophy of language. A central question is how names work. Frege and Russell both held, roughly, that ordinary proper names like 'Aristotle' work like disguised descriptions: the name means something like 'the teacher of Alexander the Great' or 'the author of the Nicomachean Ethics.' In lectures given in 1970 and published as *Naming and Necessity*, Saul Kripke attacked this view. Suppose scholars discovered that Aristotle never taught Alexander and never wrote the Ethics; we would not conclude that Aristotle did not exist, only that we had been wrong about him. Kripke argued that names are 'rigid designators' attached to their bearers by an initial 'baptism' and a chain of communication, not by descriptions. This revived a direct-reference view that Frege had rejected, and the debate continues.

On the logical side, Russell's paradox led to the development of axiomatic set theory, especially the Zermelo-Fraenkel system (ZF), which avoids the paradox by restricting which sets can be formed. ZF, with the axiom of choice, became the standard foundation of mathematics. Meanwhile, a neo-Fregean school (Crispin Wright and Bob Hale) has argued that a version of Frege's logicism can be rescued by dropping Basic Law V and starting from 'Hume's Principle,' which says two concepts have the same number when their instances can be paired one-to-one. Remarkably, Frege's own derivations of arithmetic go through from that principle. Whether the principle counts as purely logical is the sticking point.

readings.title: Logicomix: An Epic Search for Truth
readings.author: Apostolos Doxiadis and Christos H. Papadimitriou
readings.note: A graphic novel about Russell's quest for the foundations of mathematics; dramatized but a vivid introduction.

readings.title: The Problems of Philosophy
readings.author: Bertrand Russell
readings.note: A short, classic 1912 introduction written for beginners; shows the analytic method in action.

readings.title: On Sense and Reference
readings.author: Gottlob Frege
readings.note: The 1892 essay itself is short; try it in The Frege Reader, edited by Michael Beaney.

readings.title: Naming and Necessity
readings.author: Saul Kripke
readings.note: Transcribed lectures that challenged Frege and Russell on names; conversational and surprisingly readable.

questions: Is ordinary language too messy to be captured by formal logic, or does logic reveal what we really mean beneath the mess?
Should we admire Frege's logic while condemning his political views? How should we treat brilliant thinkers with ugly opinions?
Russell thought the theory of descriptions dissolved the puzzle of talking about nonexistent things. Does it work for fictional characters like Sherlock Holmes?
